newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU Commission seeks airport fees transparency.
newsitem.headline: EU Commission seeks airport fees transparency.

text.p: European Commission plans to set common rules for airport fees which will force EU airports to justify the cost and scale of charges levied, the executive said on Wednesday.

Commission proposals, to be agreed by EU transport ministers before they can become law, would mean airports would have to levy charges which were non-discriminatory for EU operators, linked directly to costs and transparent.

"At present, airport charges often do not reflect the real cost of providing airport facilities to users. At most airports, there is a considerable difference in treatment between domestic and international flights," the Commission said in a statement.
It insisted the proposal was not to harmonise charges.
"(EU) member states will be able to determine the type of charge and set their own levels provided they comply with the basic principles of the Community framework," it added.

Charges, which cover such services as aircraft landing, lighting, parking, refuelling, storage and freight services, can vary considerably between airports and account for between five and 10 percent of airlines' operating costs.
Wednesday's proposals for a legal framework for charges come as part of the EU executive's efforts to liberalise civil aviation in the EU and European Economic Area countries.
In recent months both airline operators and the airports themselves have slugged it out on the issue of charges.
The Airports Council International, which in its European region represents 300 airports in 43 countries, rejected any question of discriminatory charging at airports.
A recent ACI Europe paper said many costs related to internationally imposed norms which airports would have to absorb themselves if they could not pass on to customers.
It said complex cost structures made it impractical to calculate fees based on each facility or service used.
The Association of European Airlines, whose members include the region's major carriers, fears the proposals may be weak.
"It's one thing to have a framework but it's another to know how the framework will work," said Le Thi Mai, infrastructure specialist at the Association of European Airlines.

Le Thi, speaking ahead of Wednesday's adoption of the proposals in Commission, said the way to stop airports abusing their effective, and increasingly privatised, monopolies was to impose binding laws.
"The best way to prevent any dominance of position by private airports is to put legislation in place," she said, citing the regulations in Britain as good examples.
